# Li-Fraumeni Syndrome

**Authors:** Venkata Sushma Chamarthi, Anup Kasi

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is a rare but highly penetrant autosomal dominant cancer predisposition syndrome first described by Li and Fraumeni in 1969. This hereditary disorder is primarily caused by germline pathogenic variants in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 17p13, though variants in CHEK2 and other genes can also contribute to the syndrome. LFS is characterized by an extraordinarily high lifetime cancer risk, with recent studies demonstrating nearly 100% penetrance in females and 75% in males by age 70. The syndrome exhibits remarkable clinical heterogeneity, with 5 core cancer types comprising the majority of tumors: soft-tissue sarcomas, osteosarcomas, brain tumors, premenopausal breast cancer, and adrenocortical carcinomas. Beyond these classic malignancies, patients develop a broad spectrum of additional cancers, including leukemia, colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, lung cancer, and melanoma. The hallmark features include early age of onset (50% of cancers occur before age 40), multiple primary cancers, and strong familial clustering. Recent advances in genetic testing and clinical understanding have led to significant updates in diagnostic criteria, surveillance protocols, and emerging therapeutic strategies. Revolutionary developments in liquid biopsy technology and in the detection of somatic mosaicism are transforming clinical management, while the first chemoprevention trials offer hope for primary cancer prevention.
